title: Explicit Instruction is not the Great Equaliser of the classroom
author: Ellerton, Peter
summary: Ellerton challenges the claim that explicit instruction is the universal solution to educational equity. He argues that equityinvolves not just access to information but access to meaningful intellectual activity and development of agency. The piece distinguishes between content delivery and cultivating thinking within content, noting that both explicit instruction and inquiry-based learning can either support or suppress student thinking depending on implementation. Effective pedagogy requires professional judgment responsive to learners rather than rigid adherence to one method.
points: Equity is not only about ensuring students receive the same information in the same way, but ensuring they can use it meaningfully
Inquiry-based approaches, when properly taught, include guidance and maintain teacher control while shifting cognitive load to students
If schooling prepares some to follow instructions and others to ask questions, we have not achieved justice even if test scores are level
quotes: Equity is not only about ensuring that students receive the same information in the same way. It is also about ensuring that they can use that information meaningfully.
The common caricature of inquiry-based learning does not help. It is often portrayed as minimally guided chaos: students left to flounder while teachers stand back.

The Great Equaliser is not a particular script or sequence of moves; it is professional judgement exercised in the service of students' full intellectual flourishing.” Archived from Peter Ellerton Substack on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
